1.title: Multi-Agent Orchestration and Decomposition
1.text: Welcome to Module three: Multi-Agent Orchestration and Decomposition. This module covers multi-agent orchestration and decomposition. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. When a multi-agent design is worth its cost. The orchestrator-worker architecture and how to brief subagents. Decomposition techniques for complex problems. Production concerns: state, errors, tracing, deployment.

1.title: Case Check-In: Lumen Advisory and the Due-Diligence Research Tool
1.text: Our running case is Lumen Advisory. Lumen Advisory and the Due-Diligence Research Tool. A private-equity client wants market and regulatory research on forty companies per week. One agent runs out of context and takes hours; parallel subagents can each cover a company and a lead agent merges the findings.

1.title: When Multi-Agent Pays Off
1.text: When Multi-Agent Pays Off. Parallelism. Multi-agent fits: Independent branches (companies, sources). Single agent or workflow fits: Strong dependencies between steps. Information size. Multi-agent fits: More than one context window. Single agent or workflow fits: Fits in one window. Value of result. Multi-agent fits: High: justifies many tokens. Single agent or workflow fits: Low or routine. Shared context. Multi-agent fits: Little needed between branches. Single agent or workflow fits: Heavy shared state (most coding). Reported figures: agents use about four times the tokens of chat and multi-agent systems about fifteen times; a lead-plus-subagents design beat a single agent by about ninety percent on a research eval, and parallelization cut research time by up to ninety percent. Token usage explained most performance variance.

1.title: When Multi-Agent Pays Off, continued
1.text: When Multi-Agent Pays Off, continued. Worth it only when value, parallelism and context size justify the cost; otherwise a workflow is cheaper and simpler. Exam tip: Multi-agent is justified by parallelizable, high-value work that exceeds one context window. Tasks with heavy shared context or many dependencies (for example most coding) are poor fits.

1.title: Orchestrator-Worker Design
1.text: Orchestrator-Worker Design. The figure shows this: Orchestrator-worker architecture: a lead agent plans and delegates to parallel subagents with isolated contexts, results are verified and merged, and the plan is stored outside the context window.

1.title: Orchestrator-Worker Design, continued
1.text: Orchestrator-Worker Design, continued. Lead agent. Plans, decomposes, delegates, synthesizes; saves the plan to external memory so it survives context limits. Subagents. Own isolated context; return summaries, not raw transcripts. Brief. Give each subagent a clear objective, output format, tool guidance and task boundaries to avoid duplicated work. Effort scaling. Put explicit rules in the prompt: simple lookup equals one agent with a few tool calls; complex research equals many subagents. Verification. A separate step checks claims and attaches sources. Tools. Distinct purposes with clear descriptions; poor descriptions send agents down wrong paths.

1.title: Orchestrator-Worker Design, continued
1.text: Orchestrator-Worker Design, continued. Context isolation keeps verbose exploration out of the lead's window (Module six). Parallel tool calls inside agents cut time further. Start with broad queries and then narrow; use thinking as a planning scratchpad.

1.title: Decomposition
1.text: Decomposition. Decomposition splits a complex problem into smaller solvable parts.

1.title: Decomposition, continued
1.text: Decomposition, continued. The figure shows this: Four ways to decompose: by sequence of steps, by data partition, by role or skill, and by a dependency graph.

1.title: Decomposition, continued
1.text: Decomposition, continued. By sequence. How: Ordered steps. Example: Extract, validate, enrich, draft. By data partition. How: Split the data and run branches in parallel. Example: One subagent per company or document batch. By role. How: Specialists for skills. Example: Legal-reading agent, financial-metrics agent. By dependency. How: Graph of tasks; run independent nodes in parallel. Example: Build a plan, run in topological order. Hierarchical. How: Orchestrator decomposes at run time. Example: Unknown number of files to edit. Decompose until each part has a clear input, output and check. Minimize coupling between parts (little shared state). Define the interface between parts (schema for hand-offs). Keep human checkpoints at risky joins.

1.title: Production Concerns
1.text: Production Concerns. State and errors. Errors compound: checkpoint and resume instead of restarting; retries; let agents adapt when a tool fails. Debugging. Non-deterministic runs: trace every agent decision and tool call; monitor decision patterns. Deployment. Agents are mid-process during releases: use gradual (rainbow) deployments that shift traffic between versions. Latency. A lead that waits for each batch is a bottleneck; asynchronous designs add parallelism but also complexity. Cost control. Effort rules, step and token budgets, model tiering (cheaper subagents). Evaluation. Start with about twenty queries; L L M (large language model) judge with a rubric; judge outcomes, not fixed paths; add human testing.

1.title: Production Concerns, continued
1.text: Production Concerns, continued. Security. Per-agent least privilege; treat subagent output as untrusted data. Exam tip: For long-running agent systems the architect's answer includes checkpointing, tracing, staged deployment and step or token budgets. Exam tip: Multi-agent systems multiply tokens (about fifteen times chat): ask whether the value and parallelism justify the cost before choosing one.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Cost: Agents about four times chat tokens; multi-agent about fifteen times. Worth it: High value, parallelizable, beyond one context window. Poor fit: Heavy shared context, many dependencies (most coding). Lead agent: Plan, delegate, synthesize; save plan externally. Subagent brief: Objective, format, tool guidance, boundaries. Isolation: Own context; return summaries. Decompose: Sequence, data partition, role, dependency, hierarchical. Production: Checkpoint, trace, rainbow deploy, budgets. Evaluate: About twenty queries, L L M judge rubric, human testing.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. A research product must cover forty independent companies per week, each needing many sources. Which design is most appropriate? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Independent, high-value, context-heavy branches suit parallel subagents with isolated contexts and a lead that merges the findings.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. Which task is the poorest fit for a multi-agent design? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Shared context and many dependencies make parallel agents inefficient.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. What should a lead agent do so that the plan survives when the context fills? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. External memory outside the window is the reliable store.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Subagents are duplicating each other's searches. What is the most likely cause and fix? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Duplicated work means the briefs lack distinct objectives and task boundaries, so each subagent needs a clear scope and output format.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. A multi-agent system fails midway through a long run. What design supports recovery? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Checkpointing state lets a long run resume from the last good step instead of repeating expensive work after a failure.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. Select two. Which two are valid reasons to keep subagents' contexts isolated? The five options are on the screen. The answers are D and E. Isolation protects the lead's context and keeps hand-offs compact.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. How should a release of a long-running agent system be deployed? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Agents are mid-process, so gradual (rainbow) deployments avoid disruption.

1.title: Practice Question 8
1.text: Question eight. Which decomposition fits a task where the number of subtasks depends on the input? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. When the number of subtasks depends on the input, a run-time orchestrator must discover and assign them dynamically.

1.title: Practice Question 9
1.text: Question nine. An evaluation of a multi-agent system should begin with which approach? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Start small, grade outcomes with a rubric, and add human testing.

1.title: Practice Question 10
1.text: Question ten. Token usage of a proposed multi-agent design is about fifteen times that of a chat. Which question should the architect ask? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. The design pays off only when value and parallelism justify the token multiple.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all ten answers. Question one: C. Question two: A. Question three: D. Question four: B. Question five: C. Question six: D and E. Question seven: A. Question eight: C. Question nine: B. Question ten: B. In the next module, we continue the course.
